title: Asian Stocks Climb on Weak U.S. Jobs Data; Japan Leads Surge, Fed Hike Bets Fade
body:
Asian equity markets rallied on Monday after a softer‑than‑expected U.S. jobs report dampened expectations that the Federal Reserve will need to raise rates again this year. The data, which showed a modest slowdown in hiring and a modest rise in unemployment, helped lift technology‑heavy indices across the region and gave a boost to Japan’s market, which posted its biggest single‑day gain in months.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 surged more than 2 % to close at a level not seen since early 2022, propelled by a wave of buying in semiconductor manufacturers, consumer electronics firms and export‑oriented automakers. The rally was underpinned by a broader improvement in risk sentiment as investors reassessed the trajectory of U.S. monetary policy. In contrast, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng and Singapore’s Straits Times indices posted more modest gains of roughly 0.7 % and 0.9 % respectively, reflecting a more measured response to the same macro backdrop.

The catalyst for the market lift was the latest U.S. employment report, which showed non‑farm payrolls increasing by 150,000 jobs in June—well below the 200,000‑plus growth economists had forecast. The unemployment rate ticked up to 3.8 %, its highest level in nearly two years, while average hourly earnings grew at a slower pace. Analysts interpreted the numbers as a sign that the labor market is beginning to cool, reducing the urgency for the Fed to tighten policy further. “With the Fed’s rate‑hike cycle now looking more limited, investors are rotating back into growth‑oriented sectors,” said a senior strategist at a regional brokerage.

Technology stocks led the upside across the board. In South Korea, the KOSPI was buoyed by strong performances from chipmakers and software firms, while Taiwan’s weighted index rose on gains in major foundries and contract manufacturers. The sector’s rally was amplified by a simultaneous easing in bond yields; the 10‑year U.S. Treasury note slipped below 4.1 %, narrowing the spread that had been weighing on high‑growth equities. The lower yield environment also helped improve valuations for companies that rely heavily on future earnings, such as cloud‑computing providers and biotech firms.

Despite the overall optimism, some cautionary notes persisted. Commodity‑linked stocks in Australia and New Zealand lagged, as weaker demand forecasts for metals and agricultural products kept investors wary of a broader slowdown. Moreover, geopolitical tensions in the Indo‑Pacific region continued to hover, with recent diplomatic frictions between major powers reminding market participants that external shocks could still derail the recovery. “The rally is solid, but it’s built on a fragile macro foundation,” warned an economist at a multinational bank. “Any surprise in U.S. inflation data or a resurgence of geopolitical risk could quickly reverse sentiment.”

Looking ahead, market participants will be watching the Federal Reserve’s upcoming policy meeting for clues on the central bank’s stance. If the Fed signals a pause or a more dovish outlook, the current bullish momentum could extend into the next trading week, supporting further gains in technology and export‑driven sectors. Conversely, any indication that inflation remains stubbornly high could reignite concerns about additional rate hikes, prompting a shift back to defensive assets. For now, the combination of softer U.S. labor data and a renewed appetite for growth stocks appears to have given Asian markets a welcome lift, setting the stage for a potentially more resilient performance in the weeks to come.
